lesson.title: Reading the Signature: Factoring Perfect Square Trinomials
lesson.summary: A trinomial that passes the perfect square test, matching first and last squares with a middle term equal to twice their product, factors directly as a squared binomial.
lesson.body:
Factoring a perfect square trinomial reverses the perfect square special product covered earlier: since (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 and (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2, a trinomial matching either pattern can be factored directly as a squared binomial, without testing pairs of numbers the way a general trinomial requires.

The recognition test has three parts, the same ones used when this pattern was first introduced. Check that the first term is a perfect square, check that the last term is a perfect square, and check that the middle term equals exactly twice the product of the square roots of those two terms. If all three hold, the trinomial is a perfect square, and its sign tells you which binomial to use: a positive middle term gives (a + b)^2, while a negative middle term gives (a - b)^2.

Apply the test to x^2 - 14x + 49. The first term, x^2, has square root x. The last term, 49, has square root 7. Twice their product, 2 times x times 7, is 14x, which matches the middle term in magnitude, and since the middle term is negative, the trinomial factors as (x - 7)^2.

Check by expanding (x - 7)(x - 7): First is x times x, giving x^2. Outer is x times negative 7, giving negative 7x. Inner is negative 7 times x, giving negative 7x. Last is negative 7 times negative 7, giving 49. Adding these, x^2 - 7x - 7x + 49, the middle terms combine to negative 14x, reproducing x^2 - 14x + 49 exactly. A second example with a positive middle term and a coefficient shows the pattern still applies: 9x^2 + 12x + 4 has first term square root 3x and last term square root 2, and twice their product, 2 times 3x times 2, is 12x, matching the middle term, so it factors as (3x + 2)^2. Substituting x = 1 checks it: 9 + 12 + 4 = 25 on one side, and (3 + 2)^2 = 25 on the other.

Always run the full three part test before assuming a trinomial is a perfect square, because two matching perfect square terms are not enough on their own. Consider x^2 - 10x + 49: the first and last terms are still perfect squares, x^2 and 49, but twice the product of their roots is 14x, not the 10x actually present, so this trinomial fails the test and is not a perfect square trinomial. In that situation you would fall back on the general trinomial method, or first check for a greatest common factor, rather than forcing an incorrect squared binomial.

Perfect square trinomials also show up when solving equations, and they behave a little differently from most factored quadratics. Setting x^2 - 14x + 49 = 0 and factoring gives (x - 7)^2 = 0, and since both factors are identical, the zero product property only produces one distinct solution, x = 7, sometimes called a repeated or double root. This is different from a typical trinomial like x^2 - x - 12, which factored earlier into two different binomials and produced two different solutions.
